_comment: All the copy for /work/making-the-app-testable, in reading order. Editable in the browser under `npm run dev`, or in bulk via `npm run copy:export`. Keys are stable — renaming one orphans the string on the page. The study draws on three initiatives kept separate elsewhere (A Contextual Home, Search Experience, Small Enhancements) because they are one argument: two structural rebuilds that made testing possible, and the programme that ran through them.
title: The app that could not be tested
standfirst: Hotels.com's two most valuable screens were both fixed layouts, so nothing on them could vary and nothing could be learned from them. Rebuilding both as systems is what turned the app into something the team could run a continuous testing programme through.

contribution.detail: Senior Product Designer, covering UX, mobile and brand

The design of both rebuilds, the modular home and the dynamic card framework, across iOS and Android, along with the single brand language holding them together. Within the testing programme, I owned the variants that ran on those two screens.
Product, design, engineering and analytics, running a continuous multivariate testing programme

problem.heading: The problem
problem.standfirst: A layout that cannot vary cannot be tested, and these were the two screens where testing mattered most.
paras: Hotels.com sells in 90 points of sale and 41 languages, lists properties in over 200 countries, and takes around 165,000 bookings a day. Every one of those customers met the same two screens, a dated and static home, and a search results page built on a fixed card framework.

Both were arrangements rather than systems. Nothing on either could respond to who was looking or what they were in the middle of, and because nothing could vary, no question about what a traveller actually needed to see could be answered. The app shipped on judgement and defended it afterwards.

process.heading: How it was worked out
process.standfirst: Rebuild both screens as systems, then run everything through one programme rather than shipping one-off launches.
process.openingPara: The home moved from a fixed layout to a modular and scalable one, with a single brand language holding it together across iOS and Android, and it was the first personalisation work the company had done. Search results moved from static cards to dynamic ones, so that a card could carry different amounts of content in the same slot. Neither was a visual exercise, and both were about making the screen capable of holding a variation.

principle._note: One paragraph, three editable parts, because the middle is emphasised. Editing is plain text, so a <strong> inside a single string would be stripped the first time anyone touched it.
principle.before: What ran through them was a standing programme across product, design, engineering and analytics, built to fail fast and iterate. Its operating principle, in the words used at the time:
principle.quote: create a hypothesis to give us an opportunity to learn, not to predict.
principle.after: That distinction is what makes a losing test useful rather than embarrassing, and it is why the one below was kept rather than quietly dropped.

process.closingPara: The 2019 refresh pushed the same idea further: a global rebrand with parity across platforms, machine learning behind modules like recommended destinations and travel guides, and a shift towards content before, during and after a trip rather than only at the point of booking.
process.explorationsHeading: Three tests, and what each one settled

explorations.title: A richer image gallery, on Android
explorations.why: Won. One test, with a single fixed photograph as the control and one variant showing three. Conversion moved, gallery interaction moved by a great deal more, and the gap between those two is the part worth keeping, because it says travellers had wanted the photographs all along and the old arrangement had been rationing them to one. It also sent better-qualified shoppers through to the booking form rather than simply more of them.
explorations.imageAlt: One test on the Hotels.com property page. The control, on the left, shows a single fixed photograph badged one of 87. Variant 1, on the right, shows a three-image gallery strip badged 87, which lifts the price, rating and Book Now button up into the first screenful.

explorations.title: A search recap carrying check-in details, on iOS
explorations.why: Lost, and then lost harder. The first variant added check-in and check-out, and the second added the times as well and did worse on every measure. That shape is the finding, because the problem was never which detail we picked, it was summarising back to travellers something they had told us thirty seconds earlier.
explorations.imageAlt: The iOS search recap test: a control, and two variants adding check-in and check-out details above the lowest-priced room, with conversion, engagement, attention and confidence figures beneath each.

explorations.title: A sign-in module in the results stream
explorations.why: Unresolved. It was recorded as still running and never produced a verdict. It is here because a test without an answer is part of the record, and the alternative is a write-up in which every hypothesis conveniently resolved.
explorations.imageAlt: The sign-in module test: a control home, a variant placing a sign-in prompt above the rewards module, and a second variant that also swaps in a carousel hero image. Every measure still running.

interface.heading: The two screens
interface.standfirst: A home whose modules changed with context, and a results card that could hold a different amount of content in the same slot.
interface.mediaAlt: The Hotels.com home screen in 2014, 2016 and 2019, each shown before and after: a promotional screen of deals and app offers, then one with search and recent searches taking centre stage, then a personalised screen carrying trips, bookings and guidance.
interface.mediaCaption: Five years and three homes. The 2014 screen sells at you, the 2016 screen puts search and what you last looked at first, and by 2019 the screen opens on the trip you have already booked. Only the third of those could have been assembled differently for two different travellers.
paras: On the home, modules carried recommended destinations, travel guides and trip content, and the mix changed with context rather than staying fixed. What appeared, and in what order, became the variable, where before it had been drawn once and shipped.

On results, three adaptive layouts were built and tested against each other, each carrying a different balance of price, image and review content in the same slot. That gave us one card in three densities, with the framework underneath deciding which one a given result deserved.

slides.label: A search card laid over a destination photograph, with recently viewed beneath it.
slides.alt: The Hotels.com home on a Samsung Galaxy S3 and an iPhone 5s. A blue "Where are you going?" card sits over a full-bleed destination photograph, with a recently viewed property card below it.

slides.label: Search moves into the header, and recent searches take the top of the page.
slides.alt: The Hotels.com home on Android and an iPhone 6. The search field has moved up into the red header, with a list of recent searches below it and a "Need a hotel tonight?" card under that.

slides.label: The contextual home: a named greeting, a city guide, and the next booking.
slides.alt: The Hotels.com home on Android and an iPhone X. A named greeting and a rounded search field sit over a city photograph, followed by a guide card for the destination and the upcoming booking.

interface.resultsLabel: The results page, before, tested and after
interface.resultsCaption: The layout that existed, the three built to be tested against each other, and where results went next. The middle three are the comparison: same chrome, same filters, same three properties, and the only variable is how much space a result is worth — three fit on screen in the text-led layout, one and a half in the full-bleed one.

resultsSlides.label: Before: one fixed row, with a rating out of five and no filters above the list.
resultsSlides.alt: Hotels.com search results before the rebuild, on an iPhone X. A red header over a white bar reading "London, England, United Kingdom" with an Edit button, then "3322 properties" and a grey "Hotel Name..." field. Each result is a fixed row: name, star rating, price and an "Excellent 4.4/5" chip, with a square photograph and a pin icon at the trailing edge.

resultsSlides.label: Text-led. The name, price and score carry the card, and the photograph is held to a square.
resultsSlides.alt: The rebuilt results page with filter chips reading "Below £800", "Above 4-stars" and "Above 8.0" above a "Property name..." field. Each card runs its text down the left with a square photograph at the trailing edge: property name, a Gold Exclusive badge, star rating, distance to the city centre, price and a review score out of ten. Three results fit on screen.

resultsSlides.label: The photograph leads, and the price moves to the foot of the card.
resultsSlides.alt: The same three properties with the card reversed: the photograph sits on the leading edge and the text on the right, with the review score above a right-aligned price. Taller cards, so fewer than three results fit on screen.

resultsSlides.label: Full-bleed. One result at a time, with the badge over the photograph.
resultsSlides.alt: The same properties again with a full-width photograph across the top of each card and the text beneath it. The Gold Exclusive badge is overlaid on the image rather than sitting in the text. One and a half results fit on screen.

resultsSlides.label: After: a destination header carrying booking pressure, and the list under a tab bar.
resultsSlides.alt: A later results page opening on a photograph of London at dusk, with the dates and "81% booked for your travel dates" over it. Filter chips and "7,886 properties" sit below, then full-bleed cards showing a green review score and a price broken down as "for 1 room for 1 night including taxes and fees". A floating Filters and Map control sits above a five-icon tab bar.

impact.heading: Impact
impact.standfirst: The home's numbers are the hard ones, and the framework underneath both screens is what everything after them was tested inside.
impact.metricsSource: Hotels.com product analytics, recorded as the result of the contextual home work, on iOS and Android between 2016 and 2019. The search rebuild's own result was reported directionally rather than as figures, as a strong positive led by the US point of sale, with more customers returning within 30 days and more shortlisting.
paras: +85% on account creation beside +5% on conversion is the finding worth stating, because a contextual screen was far better at starting a relationship than at closing a booking. Sign-ins and engagement moved with account creation and point the same way. A home that knows who you are earns a reason to come back, which is a different job from selling a room today, and that is worth knowing before anyone treats personalisation as a conversion lever.

Both screens were rebuilt so they could be tested, and that worked. What the tests then asked was mostly about content and arrangement, which module, which layout and how much detail on a card, rather than whether these were the right models at all. A framework that makes variation cheap also makes it tempting to keep varying inside it, and the harder question, whether the home should have been a feed of modules in the first place, never got a hypothesis of its own.
